title: Growing-season warmth did not raise mercury in Ontario walleye and pike within lakes in 1970-2018, and autumn sampling in 1995-2004 made much of the later apparent increase
abstract: Question: do warm growing seasons raise methylmercury (Hg) in lake predatory fish, and did warming cause the post-1995 Hg increase reported for northern Ontario (Gandhi et al. 2014)? Data: Ontario Sport Fish Contaminant Monitoring Program 1970-2018 (39,914 walleye, 26,619 pike, 10,957 lake trout fillets), an independent Minnesota sample 2000-2023 without zebra-mussel exposure, and NOAA GHCN-CAMS May-September air temperature. Method: Hg at standard length per lake and year; lake and year fixed-effects tests of the prior three seasons' warmth (planned before fitting); a 1995-2004 to 2008-2018 lake comparison against local warming; and a sampling-month check. Results: +1 C changed Ontario Hg by -6.4% in walleye (95% CI -14.9 to +2.8) and -6.3% in pike (-16.6 to +5.1); a trend design gave +0.2% (-5.2 to +5.8) and -1.7% (-8.2 to +5.2). All Ontario intervals exclude the +32% per C reported for Atlantic cod. Minnesota estimates were positive but imprecise. Hg rose in southern as well as northern Ontario, although the south warmed twice as much (0.42 vs about 0.2 C), and lake Hg change did not increase with local warming (walleye -0.21, -0.56 to +0.14 per C). Within lakes, fish sampled in September-December had 8-12% less Hg than July-August fish; 69-70% of 1995-2004 lake-years were autumn samples, against 21-27% before and after. A month correction cut the mean walleye and pike increase from about 12% to 7%, and lakes sampled in the same season in both periods showed no increase. Only northern walleye kept a clear increase (+10%), in the region that warmed less. Limitations: air temperature as a proxy, small anomaly contrast after fixed effects (SD 0.16 C), a post-hoc season finding, placeholder dates for 22% of fish, no dates in the Minnesota data, and untested deposition, browning and food-web causes.

citations.reason: Reported the post-1995 increase of walleye and pike Hg in northern Ontario and proposed climate warming as a cause; we test that cause and find a sampling-season artefact.
